title: Thorne v. Dryden-Hall, (1997) 28 RFL (4th) 297
text:
FACTS

The children were infants at the date of the alleged wrongful removal. They had lived in the United Kingdom since birth. The children resided with their mother in the UK pursuant to a residence order made on 10 June 1993.

Under s. 13 of The Children Act 1989 the mother was thereby prohibited from removing the children from the jurisdiction without obtaining the written consent of every other person with parental responsibility or with the leave of the court. On 12 October 1994 the mother took the children to Canada.

On 26 October 1995 the trial judge in British Columbia found that the mother had wrongfully removed the children from their habitual residence and ordered them to be returned forthwith to the United Kingdom. 

The mother appealed to the British Columbia Court of Appeal.

---

RULING

Appeal dismissed and return ordered; the children had been wrongfully removed from their State of habitual residence.

---

GROUNDS

Rights of Custody - Art. 3

The primary objective of the Convention is the enforcement of custody rights: Thomson v. Thomson [1994] 3 SCR 551 [INCADAT cite: HC/E/CA 11]. The right to determine a child's place of residence is a custody right divisible from the right to care for the person of the child. By virtue of a non-removal clause this right may be vested in a court or in a parent who has otherwise no more than a right of access. The right to move is an incident of custody and may be granted or withheld by a judge. Article 5 defines rights of custody as including the right to determine the child's place of residence. A violation of a restriction on removal is a violation of a custody right.

In this case the residence order made under English law stated that the children live with their mother; it did not grant the mother all of the rights encompassed by the word custody. Both parents possessed the remaining parental rights and responsibilities set out in s. 3(1) of the Children Act 1989. The residence order reserved to the English Court a right of custody, the right to determine the child's place of residence. The mother's removal of the children was in breach of that right of custody and consequently wrongful.
